canonical_statement: The study aimed to estimate the reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events expected in clinical practice from adding tirzepatide to standard care.
The study used deidentified data from the Optum Clinformatics and Merative MarketScan US administrative claims databases from May 2022 through May 2025.

The analysis used an active-comparator, new-user cohort design that expanded a previously trial-benchmarked RCT-DUPLICATE framework from SURPASS-CVOT to compare tirzepatide with sitagliptin as a placebo proxy.

The fully specified protocol was preregistered before inferential analyses in the Real-World Evidence Registry and deposited in ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT07203677; amendments were documented contemporaneously.
Eligible patients were aged 40 years or older with type 2 diabetes, established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and body mass index of at least 25.

canonical_statement: Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease required evidence of previous myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, or coronary, carotid, or peripheral arterial disease identified by diagnosis codes or revascularisation procedures.

population.label: Eligible target population
inclusion_criteria: Documented qualifying ASCVD history or revascularisation evidence

canonical_statement: Patients were excluded for recent glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist or pramlintide use or for conditions predisposing to incretin-related adverse effects, including prior pancreatitis, severe gastric emptying disorders, or medullary thyroid carcinoma.

canonical_statement: Tirzepatide exposure was defined by first qualifying outpatient dispensing after a 183-day washout period.
Sitagliptin was selected as a cardiovascular outcome-neutral active comparator serving as a placebo proxy.

exposures.details: Cardiovascular outcome-neutral active comparator used as a placebo proxy

canonical_statement: The primary on-treatment follow-up began the day after cohort entry and ended at the earliest outcome, health-plan disenrollment, treatment discontinuation or switching, or one year, with a 45-day grace period for treatment changes.
MACE was defined as a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, and all cause mortality.

outcome.definition: Composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, and all cause mortality

canonical_statement: Infection related mortality was defined exploratorily as death occurring within 90 days after onset of an infection.

outcome.definition: Mortality within 90 days after infection onset

canonical_statement: The expanded cardiovascular composite included myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, and unstable angina.

outcome.definition: Myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularisation, and unstable angina

canonical_statement: Prespecified safety outcomes included infections and gastrointestinal adverse events leading to hospital admission.

outcome.definition: Infections and gastrointestinal adverse events leading to hospital admission

canonical_statement: Additional infection outcomes included infections in any care setting and urinary tract infections.

outcome.definition: Infections in any care setting and urinary tract infections

canonical_statement: Lumbar radiculopathy and abdominal hernia were prespecified as negative control outcomes to assess residual confounding.

Pretreatment covariates were selected to capture common causes of treatment assignment and outcomes, including demographic, cardiovascular, metabolic, comorbidity, medication, healthcare-utilisation, and proxy socioeconomic factors.
Propensity scores were estimated with logistic regression using all baseline covariates and applied through overlap weighting to emphasise patients with greatest clinical equipoise.
Covariate balance was assessed with standardised mean differences, with values below 0.1 considered acceptable.
Weighted Kaplan-Meier methods estimated event-free survival and overlap-weighted Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Analyses were performed separately in the two claims databases and pooled with fixed-effects meta-analysis weighted by effective sample size.

Number needed to treat was calculated as the reciprocal of the weighted one-year absolute risk difference, assuming an unconfounded risk difference, non-informative censoring, and transportability to similar populations.
A prespecified as-started sensitivity analysis carried initial treatment assignment forward for up to one year as an intention-to-treat analogue.
A competing-risk sensitivity analysis treated death as a competing event for non-fatal outcomes using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models.
Predefined subgroup analyses included age and sex, with additional exploratory subgroup analyses reported by BMI and concomitant SGLT2 inhibitor or insulin use.
The source cohort included 52,971 individuals: 35,353 initiators of tirzepatide and 17,618 initiators of sitagliptin.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that adding tirzepatide to standard care was associated with a lower risk of MACE than adding the cardiovascular-neutral placebo proxy sitagliptin.

The authors proposed that reductions in serious infections and infection related mortality might explain part of the observed survival benefit through non-atherosclerotic pathways; they described this as a hypothesis requiring substantiation.
The authors cautioned that mortality findings may be affected by residual confounding because prior benchmarking suggested DPP-4 inhibitors can be preferentially prescribed to frailer patients.
Follow-up was limited to one year and median on-treatment follow-up was less than half a year, potentially underestimating longer term cardiovascular and safety effects.
Sitagliptin was used as a placebo proxy despite differing from tirzepatide in route of administration, which can contribute to treatment channeling.
Residual confounding from unmeasured factors could not be excluded despite comprehensive overlap weighting and might partly explain the mortality reduction and rapid onset of cardiovascular benefit.
Administrative claims algorithms could misclassify treatment duration or outcomes, and the study did not observe dose or timing of treatment escalation.
The expanded composite including revascularisation and unstable angina may be more sensitive to clinical decision making and surveillance intensity than hard cardiovascular endpoints.
The findings may not generalise to uninsured patients, non-US healthcare systems, or patients without established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

The authors concluded that trial-anchored real-world evidence can complement randomised clinical trials for timely regulatory and clinical decision making while further tirzepatide cardiovascular trial evidence accrues.

The study was funded by the US National Institutes of Health and the German Heart Foundation; the authors reported that funders had no role in design, analysis, interpretation, writing, or publication decisions.

The authors disclosed institutional grants or contracts and consulting relationships, including SVW consulting for Cytel, Exponent, and MITRE and SS consulting for Aetion, all described as unrelated to the submitted work.

Patient-level claims data cannot be publicly shared under data use agreements; access may be requested from the data vendors, and the analytical code used to generate tables, figures, and statistical results is publicly available.
The Mass General Brigham institutional review board approved the study, and use of deidentified secondary data qualified for a waiver of informed consent.
